44.title: The Public Ministry of Jesus
44.001.h3: 1. Preparation and Beginning of the Public Ministry (A.D. 26)
44.003.p: The public ministry of Jesus officially began in January, A.D. 26, when he was baptized by John the Baptist near Pella in the Jordan River [135:8.1]. When Jesus was baptized, a voice from heaven was heard saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" [135:8.6], and this event became the decisive moment when he undertook his mission as the Son of Man while simultaneously realizing his divinity as the Son of God, and from this time on, an undoubting confidence in his divine nature took possession of his human consciousness [136:2.6]. After baptism, Jesus spent forty days in isolation in the hills to commune with the Father and determine the course of his future ministry, which was not merely a fast but a significant period of spiritual preparation involving cosmic testing with the rebels of the System of Satania [136:3.1].
44.004.h4: 2) Selection of the First Apostles and the Event of Turning Water into Wine
44.005.p: Early in his ministry, Jesus chose his first apostles, including Andrew, Peter, James, and John, making them associates of the Kingdom of God [137:1.1]. Later, at the wedding feast in Cana, the event of turning water into wine occurred, which was not a miracle intended by Jesus but a creative act that transcended the time element and abridged natural processes [137:4.13], and due to this event, the disciples believed in him as the Messiah, and their expectations regarding his ministry were heightened [137:4.16].
44.006.h3: 2. Ordination and Training of the Twelve (A.D. 27)
44.008.p: On January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus formally ordained the twelve apostles and established them as ambassadors of the Kingdom of God [140:0.1]. Prior to the ordination, Jesus presented the spiritual attitudes and ethical standards the apostles should possess through a sermon often called the 'Sermon on the Mount,' which included the Beatitudes starting with "Happy are the poor in spirit" and was a revolutionary declaration emphasizing inner motives and love rather than external legal observance [140:3.3]. This ordination was a crucial turning point where the apostles transformed from mere disciples into an organized core group that would inherit and expand Jesus' ministry.
44.010.p: After ordination, the apostles lived with Jesus and received intensive training, during which Jesus taught them to focus on preaching the gospel and spiritually healing people rather than performing miracles [138:6.1]. Jesus sent the apostles out in pairs to gain practical experience and commanded them, "Freely you have received, freely give," urging them to serve only without expecting material rewards [140:9.2].
44.011.h4: 3) Sabbath Controversies and Hostility of the Pharisees
44.012.p: As Jesus' ministry became active, conflicts with Jewish religious leaders surfaced, particularly acts such as healing the sick on the Sabbath or disciples plucking grain to eat, which directly clashed with the legalism of the Pharisees [147:6.4]. Jesus declared, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath" [147:6.4], proclaiming that human need and mercy take precedence over religious forms. These teachings and actions were perceived as challenges to existing religious authority, amplifying the hostility of the Pharisees and Sadducees, which later became one of the decisive causes leading to his crucifixion [148:9.3].
44.013.h3: 3. Crisis and Transition: Height of Ministry and Rejection (A.D. 28 ~ 29)
44.014.h4: 1) Preaching Tours and Attitude Toward Miracles
44.015.p: In January, A.D. 28, Jesus began his first public preaching tour in Galilee and preached the gospel in many cities, excluding Nazareth [146:0.1]. During this period, Jesus intentionally tried not to perform miracles, but phenomena of healing occurred due to the combination of people's strong faith and Jesus' creative power [149:1.1]. Jesus emphasized that miracles were not the essence of gospel preaching and wanted people to realize spiritual truths rather than seeking signs [145:5.6].
44.016.h4: 2) Feeding the Five Thousand and Refusal of Kingship
44.017.p: In March, A.D. 29, Jesus performed the supernatural event of feeding a crowd of five thousand near Bethsaida-Julias [152:2.9]. This event caused the crowd's enthusiasm to reach its peak, attempting to force him to be king, but Jesus firmly refused, saying, "My kingdom is not of this world," and dismissed them [152:3.2]. This event became a major watershed in Jesus' public ministry; the masses who expected material prosperity and political liberation were disappointed and began to leave him, and Jesus' ministry transitioned from popular popularity to the stage of training true spiritual disciples [152:5.2].
44.018.h4: 3) Peter's Confession and Declaration at Caesarea-Philippi
44.019.p: After the public support disappeared, Jesus asked the apostles at Caesarea-Philippi, "Who do you say that I am?" and Peter confessed, "You are the Son of the living God" [157:3.5]. This confession was a significant event showing that the apostles began to recognize Jesus as a being possessing divinity beyond a mere Messiah, and Jesus declared he would build the kingdom of spiritual brotherhood upon this rock of faith [157:4.5]. Afterward, Jesus began to openly predict that he would suffer and be killed in Jerusalem.
44.020.h4: 4) Transfiguration and the Glory of the Son of Man
44.021.p: A few days after Peter's confession, Jesus took Peter, James, and John up Mount Hermon and was transfigured, where he conversed with celestial beings and revealed his divine glory [158:1.8]. This event was part of the process of Jesus acquiring universal sovereignty [158:3.2] and was an important experience that instilled confidence in Jesus' divinity in the apostles ahead of the coming suffering of the cross. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus charged them, "Tell no man what you have seen until the Son of Man has risen from the dead" [158:2.1].
44.022.h4: 5) Mission of the Seventy and Perea Ministry
44.023.p: Having finished the Galilean ministry, Jesus appointed seventy evangelists and sent them to the Perea region across the Jordan [163:1.1]. This was intended to extend gospel preaching not only to Jews but also to Gentiles [163:4.2], and to provide an opportunity for salvation to more people on the final journey toward Jerusalem. The seventy proclaimed, "The kingdom of heaven has come near," healed the sick, and preached the gospel [163:1.4], and their ministry achieved great success, leading many to accept the gospel.
44.025.h4: 1) Resurrection of Lazarus and the Sanhedrin's Resolution of Death
44.026.p: In March, A.D. 30, Jesus revealed his divinity most powerfully by raising the dead Lazarus [168:2.7]. This event caused many to believe but simultaneously became the decisive moment for the Sanhedrin to officially resolve to kill Jesus [168:3.2]. The Jewish leaders judged that if they did not eliminate Jesus, their authority would collapse.
44.027.h4: 2) Entry into Jerusalem and Cleansing of the Temple
44.028.p: In April, A.D. 30, Jesus entered Jerusalem riding on a donkey, which symbolized his coming as the King of Peace [172:3.4]. The crowd welcomed him shouting "Hosanna" [172:3.9], but Jesus challenged the authority of the religious leaders head-on by entering the temple, driving out those who sold, and cleansing the temple [173:1.7]. This event exploded the anger of the Sanhedrin and accelerated the process of their resolution to kill Jesus [173:2.2].
44.029.h4: 3) Last Supper and Prayer in Gethsemane
44.030.p: On the night before the Passover, Jesus shared the last supper with the apostles, showing an example of humility by washing their feet [179:3.7], and established the new covenant ceremony of remembrance through bread and wine [179:5.9]. Afterward, in the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed, "Not my will, but yours be done," overcoming the fear of death he faced as a human through faith and completely obeying the Father's will [182:3.4]. Here he was arrested through Judas's betrayal [183:3.5].
44.032.p: Jesus was interrogated through Jewish religious trials and Pilate's Roman court, and although Pilate found no fault in him, he permitted the crucifixion due to crowd pressure and political reasons [185:8.1]. Jesus was nailed to the cross on Golgotha, and even in extreme pain, he practiced love and forgiveness by praying, "Father, forgive them" [187:2.4]. He ended his physical life with the words "It is finished" [187:5.5]. His death was not a sacrificial offering for sin, but a confirmation of God's love for man and a demonstration of the way of eternal life that overcomes even death [188:5.2].
44.033.h4: 5) Resurrection, Ascension, and Descent of the Spirit of Truth
44.034.p: Early Sunday morning, three days after the crucifixion, Jesus rose from the dead [189:1.1]. The resurrected Jesus appeared in morontia (spiritual) form to Mary, the apostles, and many disciples to prove the reality of the resurrection and comfort them. After a period of appearances, Jesus ascended [193:5.3], and on Pentecost, poured out the promised 'Spirit of Truth' upon all flesh [194:0.1]. With this, Jesus' physical ministry ended, but a new era opened where he dwells eternally in the hearts of all believers through the Spirit of Truth, guiding them into truth [194:3.1].
45.title: The Kingdom of Heaven of Jesus
45.001.h3: 1. The Nature and Basic Concepts of the Kingdom of Heaven
45.003.p: The Kingdom of Heaven as proclaimed by Jesus was not a material kingdom of this world, nor was it a political government to re-establish the rule of Israel and sit on the throne of David [137:8.7]. The Kingdom of Heaven consists in the realization and acknowledgment of the rule of God within the human heart, and indeed there is a King in this kingdom, and that King is the Father of Jesus and the Father of all believers [141:2.1]. Jesus taught that the kingdom is not said to be here or there, but rather "the Kingdom of God is within you," explaining that where the spirit of God teaches and leads the soul of man, there in reality is the kingdom of heaven [137:8.9]. This kingdom is not a matter of meat and drink, but rather righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit [137:8.10].
45.004.h4: 2) The Fatherhood of God and the Brotherhood of Man
45.005.p: The gospel of the Kingdom of Heaven is founded on the truth of the fatherhood of God and the correlated fact of the brotherhood of man [170:2.1]. Jesus sought to substitute the concept of the kingdom, king, and subjects with the concept of the heavenly family, the heavenly Father, and the liberated sons of God engaged in joyful and voluntary service for their fellow men and in sublime worship of God the Father [170:2.12]. God is not the God of the Jew or the Gentile, for all are his children, and when one believes this new gospel of divine sonship, the Father's will becomes their will, and they are elevated to become the liberated sons of the kingdom [141:2.2].
45.006.h4: 3) The Dual Concept of the Kingdom
45.007.p: Jesus taught the kingdom as a dual concept, being both a present reality and a future hope [170:1.4]. The kingdom was a matter of personal experience already existing in the hearts of true believers, while at the same time being a matter of racial or world phenomena to be looked forward to in the future [170:2.13]~15. Jesus described the Kingdom of God in this world as the supreme desire to do the will of God, and the Kingdom of God in heaven as the goal of mortal believers, a state where God's love is perfected and his will is divinely done [170:2.18]~19.
45.008.h3: 2. Five Phases of the Kingdom of Heaven
45.010.p: The kingdom taught by Jesus embraces five phases or epochs, the first being the personal and inward experience of the spiritual life of the individual believer in fellowship with God the Father [170:4.2]. This means that the religion of Jesus is personal and individual, and the kingdom begins with the individual's inner experience of attaining righteousness through faith and finding God [170:3.10].
45.011.h4: 2) The Social Aspect of Enlarged Brotherhood
45.012.p: The second phase is the enlarged brotherhood of gospel believers, the social aspects of the enhanced morals and quickened ethics resulting from the reign of God's spirit in the hearts of individual believers [170:4.3]. The religion of the kingdom is personal, but its fruits and results are familial and social, and the fellowship of believers reveals itself in the paths of social service [170:3.8].
45.014.p: The third is the supermortal brotherhood of invisible spiritual beings which prevails on earth and in Paradise, the superhuman kingdom of God [170:4.4]. This is characterized by the unity of invisible spiritual beings and signifies the spiritual unity that is the fruit of faith-union with the living Jesus [195:10.11].
45.015.h4: 4) The Prospect of a New Social Order
45.016.p: The fourth is the prospect of the more perfect fulfillment of the will of God, the advance toward the dawn of a new social order in connection with improved spiritual living—the next age of man [170:4.5].
45.017.h4: 5) The Age of Light and Life
45.018.p: The fifth is the kingdom in its perfection, the future spiritual age of light and life on earth [170:4.6]. Jesus taught that when the gospel of the kingdom has been preached to all the world and salvation has spread to all peoples, the world will pass through the long winter of materialism and the spiritual springtime of a new age will approach.
45.019.h3: 3. Conditions for Entry and Life in the Kingdom
45.021.p: The only requirement for entering the kingdom of heaven is faith [138:8.8]. Jesus taught that unless one seeks to enter the kingdom with the faith of a little child and a trusting heart, one shall in no wise enter therein. Entering the kingdom is wholly a free gift, bestowed upon all who have faith to receive sonship in the family of God.
45.023.p: While faith is the key to entering the kingdom, the way to live within the kingdom is to do the will of the Father in heaven [140:1.4]. When the Father's will becomes one's law, one is a noble servant, but when the Father's will truly becomes one's will, one is a son in the kingdom [141:2.2]. Jesus taught his disciples to pray, "Your kingdom come; your will be done" [170:2.11].
45.025.p: The righteousness of the kingdom is not a negative righteousness of keeping laws or taboos, but a positive righteousness consisting of love, mercy, and truth [140:6.3]. Jesus positively interpreted the commandment "Love your neighbor as yourself" to mean doing unto others as you would have them do unto you, which signifies active service of overcoming evil with good, rather than passive non-resistance [159:5.14]. The citizens of the kingdom must be the salt of the earth and the light of the world [140:4.2], and those who enter the kingdom receive the rewards of altruistic service [137:8.11].
45.027.p: The gospel of the kingdom is about liberation from the bondage of fear and ritual, enjoying the liberty and joy of the children of God. The citizens of the kingdom shall know the truth, and the truth shall make them free [162:7.2]. This joy is not in the abundance of material possessions but comes from spiritual progress and divine communion [140:1.4].
45.030.p: Jesus taught, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's," clarifying that there is no fundamental conflict between the spiritual kingdom and secular government [178:1.3]. A believer of the kingdom should be a good citizen of the secular government, but should not use secular power or physical force to advance the spiritual kingdom [178:1.6]. Since his kingdom is not of this world, his disciples do not fight [185:3.3].
45.032.p: The kingdom is not a political or economic reform movement [140:8.10]. Jesus did not condemn wealth itself but warned against the love of wealth and greed hindering spiritual life, teaching that one cannot serve two masters [163:3.1]. The kingdom does not enforce social equality but proclaims that all are spiritually equal before God [134:4.7].
45.033.h3: 5. Transition of the Kingdom Concept and Christianity
45.035.p: The Jews expected a material kingdom where the Messiah would restore the throne of David and defeat the Gentiles to bring national prosperity [141:2.1]. However, Jesus rejected these material expectations and emphasized that the kingdom is a spiritual reality within the human heart [170:2.17]~19.
45.036.p: 2) Emergence of the Church and Change in Kingdom Concept: After Jesus' death, the disciples transformed Jesus' teaching of the kingdom into a religion about Jesus [194:4.5]. Instead of the gospel of the kingdom—the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man—they focused on proclaiming the risen Christ [194:0.4]. Paul's institutionalized church virtually became a substitute for the kingdom of heaven proclaimed by Jesus, and the kingdom was postponed to the future, to appear at the second coming of Christ [170:5.7].
45.038.p: The so-called Christian church is like the cocoon in which the concept of Jesus' spiritual kingdom lies sleeping; eventually, the kingdom of divine brotherhood will emerge [170:5.21]. The true kingdom contained in Jesus' teachings still exists in the hearts of believers, and someday other great teachers will arise to proclaim this original gospel of the kingdom—the spiritual reality of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man [170:5.19].
46.title: The Christology of the Urantia Book
46.001.h3: 1. Identity of Jesus: Creator and Sovereign of Nebadon
46.002.h4: 1) Unique Status as a Creator Son
46.003.p: Unlike Christian theology, which identifies Jesus with the Eternal Son (the second person of the Trinity), The Urantia Book clearly distinguishes that Jesus is not the Eternal Son of Paradise [33:1.2]. Jesus is a Son of God of the "Michael" order, the Creator and Sovereign of the local universe of Nebadon. Within the person of the Creator Son, the Universal Father and the Eternal Son are present, and to his universe and all its inhabited worlds, the Creator Son is, to all practical intents and purposes, God [33:1.4].
46.004.h4: 2) Absolute Authority within the Local Universe
46.005.p: The Michael Son embodies and represents all the divine attributes and powers of the Universal Father and the Eternal Son within the local universe [33:1.2]. He was already the Creator of the universe before coming to Urantia in the flesh, and through seven bestowals, he acquired supreme sovereignty over his universe [21:4.5]. Therefore, he is more than just the savior of humanity; he is the Father and Ruler of our universe [33:1.4].
46.006.h3: 2. Purpose of the Earth Mission: Revelation and Sovereignty
46.007.h4: 1) Completion of Creature Experience and Acquiring Sovereignty
46.008.p: The primary purpose of Jesus coming to earth (Urantia) was to complete his experience as a creature by living a mortal life in the flesh, thereby acquiring full sovereignty over his universe [120:0.1]. This was a necessary process for the Creator to become a just and merciful ruler by directly experiencing the life of his creatures, and his death on Urantia was the final step in completing his bestowal career [21:4.5].
46.009.h4: 2) Mutual Revelation of God and Man
46.010.p: Another purpose was to perfectly reveal God the Father to men and simultaneously reveal man to God through his life in the flesh [120:2.8]. He demonstrated the love and mercy of God on this earth and set an example of the divine life attainable by man [120:2.8]. This was to exhibit, within a short life in the flesh, the transcendent phenomenon of God seeking and finding man, and man seeking and finding God, to the mutual satisfaction of both [120:2.8].
46.011.h3: 3. The Seven Great Salvations Provided by Jesus' Faith
46.012.h4: 1) Salvation from Material, Intellectual, and Spiritual Bondage
46.013.p: The faith of Jesus pointed the way to the finality of human salvation and the ultimate of mortal universe attainment [101:6.8]. First, it offers salvation from material fetters by the realization of sonship with God, who is spirit [101:6.9]. Second, it offers salvation from intellectual bondage: man shall know the truth, and the truth shall set him free [101:6.10]. Third, it offers salvation from spiritual blindness, the realization of the fraternity of mortal beings and the brotherhood of all universe creatures, leading to the service-discovery of spiritual reality and the revelation of the goodness of spiritual values [101:6.11].
46.014.h4: 2) Perfection of Self and Transcendence of Limitations
46.015.p: Salvation is also a journey toward self-completion. Fourth, it offers salvation from incompleteness of self through the attainment of the spirit levels of the universe and the realization of the harmony of Havona and the perfection of Paradise [101:6.12]. Fifth, it offers salvation from self, deliverance from the limitations of self-consciousness through the attainment of the cosmic levels of the Supreme mind and coordination with the attainments of all other self-conscious beings [101:6.13].
46.017.p: Sixth, it offers salvation from time, the achievement of an eternal life of unending progression in God-recognition and God-service [101:6.14]. Seventh, it offers salvation from the finite, the perfected oneness with Deity in and through the Supreme by which the creature attempts the transcendental discovery of the Ultimate [101:6.15].
46.018.h3: 4. The Seven Elements Provided by Jesus' Religion
46.019.p: Harmonious Integration and Inner Assurance: The religion Jesus preached was the first Urantian religion to harmoniously integrate knowledge, wisdom, faith, truth, and love [101:6.8]. This religion provided believers with seven essential inner assurances:
46.020.p: 1) Temporal tranquility: Jesus' teachings harmoniously coordinated knowledge, wisdom, faith, truth, and love to provide tranquility in time [101:6.8].
46.021.p: 2) Intellectual assurance: His religion provided firm faith and assurance even in the intellectual realm [101:6.8].
46.022.p: 3) Moral enlightenment: The faith of Jesus became a light providing moral enlightenment [101:6.8].
46.023.p: 4) Philosophic stability: His teachings brought philosophic stability to life and the universe [101:6.8].
46.024.p: 5) Ethical sensitivity: The religion of Jesus cultivated the ability to react and act with ethical sensitivity [101:6.8].
46.025.p: 6) God-consciousness: His teachings led to a deep consciousness and recognition of God [101:6.8].
46.026.p: 7) Positive assurance of personal survival: The faith of Jesus provided a definite assurance of personal survival after death [101:6.8].
46.027.p: Jesus' teachings do not confine man to fear or uncertainty but elevate the quality of life and qualify him for cosmic citizenship through these elements.
46.028.h3: 5. Meaning of the Cross: Rejection of Atonement and Victory of Love
46.029.h4: 1) Rejection of Atonement Doctrine and Nature of God
46.030.p: The Urantia Book firmly rejects the traditional Christian doctrine of atonement, which teaches that Jesus was sacrificed to appease God's wrath for the sins of humanity [4:5.4], [188:4.1]. God is a Father of love, not an angry deity who requires the blood of a sinless son for forgiveness [4:5.6]. Salvation is not a flight from divine wrath but the realization of sonship with God [141:2.2].
46.031.h4: 2) The Cross as Human Act and Divine Love
46.032.p: The crucifixion was not required by God but was an act committed by the ignorance and prejudice of men [186:5.2]. Jesus' death was not the payment of a debt but the supreme expression of love and forgiveness in the face of human hatred and evil [188:5.6]. The cross is not a sacrificial altar but an eternal symbol showing how great and persistent God's love is, despite human wickedness [188:5.7].
46.033.h3: 6. Relationship with Us: Brother, Friend, and Indwelling Spirit
46.035.p: Jesus is our Creator and Sovereign, yet because he lived a life in the flesh like ours, he has become our true brother and friend [127:6.13]. He opened a "new and living way" for us to approach God [52:5.4] and brought about a change in spiritual status whereby we know God as Father and accept ourselves as his children.
46.036.h4: 2) Continued Presence through the Spirit of Truth
46.037.p: After his ascension, he sent the "Spirit of Truth" to all flesh, remaining spiritually with us [120:2.6], [194:3.1]. Through Jesus, we know God, and through the Spirit he sent, we are guided into truth. The faith of Jesus was nourished by and revealed a reality beyond the ultimate; thus, by following his faith, we can potentially attain the reality of faith in human religious experience [101:6.16].
47.title: The Twelve Apostles of Jesus
47.002.h3: 1. The Call and Solemn Ordination of the Twelve
47.004.p: On Sunday, January 12, A.D. 27, Jesus called the apostles together to ordain them as public preachers of the gospel of the kingdom [140:0.1]. Jesus walked along the shore calling them two by two, starting with Andrew and Peter who were fishing, and James and John who were mending nets, and when all twelve were gathered, they went up to the highlands north of Capernaum for instruction prior to the official ordination [140:0.2]. The apostles felt that the long-awaited moment had arrived and fell into deep silence and meditation, participating in a solemn ceremony of consecration to a divine mission [140:0.3].
47.006.p: Jesus instructed the disciples to kneel in a circle about him, and then he placed his hands upon the head of each apostle, beginning with Judas Iscariot and ending with Andrew [140:2.1]. Through prayer, Jesus dedicated them to the Father, stating that just as he came to represent the Father, he was sending them forth to represent him, and he committed all the interests of the coming kingdom into their hands [140:2.2]. After the prayer, the disciples remained with bowed heads in a great silence, and then, rising one by one, they embraced Jesus, but no man spoke [140:2.3].
47.007.h4: 3) The Ordination Sermon (Sermon on the Mount)
47.008.p: The so-called "Sermon on the Mount" was actually the ordination charge given by Jesus to the twelve apostles, a personal commission to those chosen to represent him in the world [140:4.1]. Jesus reminded the apostles that they were the salt of the earth and the light of the world, emphasizing that they were called to save men, not to judge them [140:3.12], [140:3.13], [140:3.17].
47.009.h3: 2. Personalities, Relationships with Jesus, and Peculiarities
47.011.p: At the moment of ordination, Peter was so overcome with awe that he was lost in deep thought and hardly dared look up at the Master [140:2.3]. During the training, he asked about the "new commandment," eliciting the teaching that values motives above acts and warns against the dangers of anger and hatred [140:6.4]. Near the end of the training, Peter, along with James, expressed confidence saying, "We are ready, let us go forth to conquer the kingdom," but Jesus cautioned his excessive zeal, saying, "May your wisdom equal your zeal" [140:7.7]. He sought a private interview with Jesus because his mind was troubled, fearing he might have done something to deserve a rebuke [140:6.14]. Peter grasped the concept that the gospel was a "new beginning" for the whole human race, a concept he later passed on to Paul [140:8.24].
47.013.p: Andrew took on the practical role of organizing the apostles and assigning visitors [140:7.2]. On the evening of the ordination, he acted as a mediator, confessing that his brethren could not understand the teachings and leading Jesus to the garden for further instruction [140:6.1]. He also showed consideration for his brothers by asking Jesus if he should wake the twins when they fell asleep during the late-night interviews, to which Jesus reassured him that "they are doing well" [140:6.14]. Andrew learned that the morality of Jesus could not be separated from the religion of his life [140:10.8].
47.014.h4: 3) James Zebedee (Seeker of Norms and Truth)
47.015.p: James asked questions about social rules such as divorce, but Jesus clarified that he was not a lawgiver but came to set free the souls of men [140:6.6]. James was active enough to say "we are ready" along with Peter [140:7.7], and along with Peter and John, received special private instruction from Jesus [140:8.1]. James grasped the truth that Jesus wanted his children on earth to live as though they were already citizens of the completed heavenly kingdom [140:8.25].
47.016.h4: 4) John Zebedee (Understanding of Love and Spirit)
47.017.p: John was one of the three to receive special instruction, charged with clarifying Jesus' mind to his associates. He asked, "What is the kingdom of heaven?" and learned that its essence lies in the recognition of God's sovereignty, belief in sonship, and the desire to do God's will [140:10.9]. John deeply understood that the religion of Jesus consists in the acquiring of a compassionate character coupled with a personality bent on doing the will of the Father [140:8.23].
47.019.p: Thomas, full of doubt and caution, asked if they should own everything in common, to which Jesus taught that one cannot serve God and mammon simultaneously [140:6.13]. He even suggested delaying their departure, fearing they were not yet able to perform their duties [140:7.1]. Thomas also asked about the confusion between becoming "as a little child" and "bewaring of false prophets," leading Jesus to explain the trust relationship between Father and child [140:10.4].
47.021.p: Nathaniel struggled with the conflict between the Mosaic law of "an eye for an eye" and Jesus' teaching of non-resistance, asking about the question of justice [140:6.9]. Jesus taught him that apostles, unlike human rulers, must return good for evil and let mercy determine their judgments [140:6.9]. When Jesus offered them the chance to go back if the teaching was too hard, it became the catalyst for the apostles, led by Peter, to resolve to follow him [140:6.10].
47.023.p: During supper, Matthew learned from Jesus that the morality of any act is determined by the individual's motive [140:10.5]. Jesus taught Matthew a positive morality requiring active social contact, reinterpreting the Golden Rule [140:10.5].
47.025.p: Simon asked, "Are all men the sons of God?" confronting the shocking truth of universal brotherhood which was difficult for a Jew of that time to accept [140:10.7]. Jesus confirmed to him that all men are sons of God and that this is the good news they were to preach [140:10.7].
47.027.p: Judas was the first to be ordained [140:2.1]. He received specific instructions regarding the disbursement of alms, being told to pay out funds only upon the request of Jesus or the joint petition of two other apostles, to avoid the social evils of indiscriminate kindness [140:8.13].
47.029.p: The twins showed simple faithfulness rather than deep theological concern. While other apostles went for private interviews with Jesus throughout the night, they fell asleep by the fire, and Jesus told Andrew, "They are doing well—do not disturb them" [140:6.14].
47.030.h3: 3. Forecast of Future Fate and Mission
47.032.p: On the day of consecration, Jesus sent the disciples into the world, describing them as "sheep in the midst of wolves" [140:9.3]. Jesus advised them to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, predicting specific trials ahead [140:9.3]. They would be brought before councils, rebuked in synagogues, and stand before governors and rulers [140:9.3].
47.034.p: Jesus clearly told the apostles, "Some of you will be put to death, and before you establish the kingdom on earth, you will be hated by many peoples for the sake of this gospel" [140:9.3]. This implied that the individual fates of the apostles would not be smooth and that a time would come when they would have to lay down their lives for the gospel.
47.036.p: Although their bodies might be persecuted and killed, Jesus promised, "I will be with you, and my spirit shall go before you into all the world" [140:9.3]. He also encouraged them not to worry about what to say when judged, for the spirit of the Father would speak through them [140:9.3]. Jesus emphasized that what they were—their relationship of sonship with God—was more important than what they did, reminding them of the essence of their future ministry [140:10.1].
48.title: Jesus' Three Preaching Tours
48.001.h3: 1. The First Preaching Tour in Galilee and Major Events
48.002.h4: 1) Start of the Tour and Teachings at Rimmon
48.003.p: The first public preaching tour in Galilee began on Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, continuing for about two months, during which Jesus and the twelve apostles, assisted by John's former disciples, preached the gospel in Rimmon, Jotapata, Ramah, and other cities [146:0.1]. This tour was the first opportunity Jesus permitted his associates to preach without restraint, and the apostles felt great satisfaction in the fact that they could freely preach and teach the gospel [146:0.2]. At Rimmon, Jesus clearly explained the difference between the new gospel of the kingdom and the old beliefs of the people who worshiped the Babylonian air god, Ramman [146:1.1]. Here, Todan heard the gospel of the kingdom for the first time, and he later became one of the first to carry the message beyond the Euphrates River into Mesopotamia [146:1.4].
48.005.p: The mission at Jotapata was special because Jesus preached a detailed sermon on prayer to the twenty-four believers, teaching that harboring iniquity in the human heart disrupts the spiritual connection circuit and that prayers inconsistent with God's laws are an abomination to the deities [146:2.3]. Jesus emphasized that although God has already forgiven, in human experience, divine forgiveness becomes available only when one forgives their fellows [146:2.4]. Furthermore, he taught that prayer is not a technique for transcending time or aggrandizing the self, and the only form of prayer appropriate for God's children is "Nevertheless, your will be done" [146:2.9][146:2.12]. Jesus advised them to extend their capacity to receive the presence of the inner divine spirit through prayer and to pray with a spirit of thanksgiving [146:2.15].
48.006.h4: 3) The Leper at Iron and Healing of the Nobleman's Son
48.007.p: At Iron, Jesus spent his time working with the miners, where a leper, hearing of Jesus' fame, came and begged for healing [146:4.3]. Jesus touched him and said, "Be made clean," and immediately he was healed; this constituted the first so-called miracle that Jesus intentionally performed [146:4.3][146:4.5]. At Cana, Titus, a nobleman of Capernaum, came for his critically ill son, and Jesus told him, "Your son will live," and on his way home, Titus learned that the boy had recovered [146:5.2]. People regarded this as a miracle, but it was an utilization of foreknowledge of natural laws and not a miracle of physical healing [146:5.2].
48.008.h4: 4) The Widow's Son at Nain and Teaching at Endor
48.009.p: Near the gate of Nain, Jesus met a funeral procession and, seeing the widow's dead son, perceived that he was not really dead but in a coma [146:6.2]. Jesus commanded, "Arise," and woke the boy, but the crowd was seized with extreme emotional excitement, believing Jesus had performed a miracle of raising the dead [146:6.2]~3. To escape this clamor, Jesus moved to Endor, where he taught the apostles that the spirits of the dead cannot communicate with the living and explained that rebellious midwayers would be brought under control [146:7.1]~2.
48.010.h3: 2. The Bethsaida Training Period and Events of the Jerusalem Visit
48.011.h4: 1) Visit to Jerusalem and Sabbath Controversy
48.012.p: During the interval between tours, Jesus visited Jerusalem, where at the pool of Bethesda, he preached to the afflicted that spiritual healing and faith in sonship with God were more important than physical healing [147:3.3]. Also, at the house of Simon the Pharisee, when a sinful woman washed Jesus' feet, Jesus used the parable that one who is forgiven much loves much to forgive her sins and point out Simon's pride [147:5.4]. On the way back to Capernaum, when the disciples were criticized for plucking and eating grain on the Sabbath, Jesus declared, "The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath," proclaiming that the Sabbath was made for man [147:6.4].
48.013.h4: 2) Evangelist Training at Bethsaida and Hospital
48.014.p: Operation For about five months at Bethsaida, an evangelist training school and a hospital were operated; Peter was in charge of the school, and Elman, a Syrian physician, managed the hospital, treating the sick with prayer and faith [148:2.1]. During this time, Jesus was frequently absent doing "the Father's business," which involved directing phases of universe administration [148:3.2]. During this training, Jesus taught Thomas the important distinction that evil is unconscious transgression, sin is conscious transgression, and iniquity is persistent rebellion [148:4.3]~5.
48.015.h4: 3) Understanding Suffering and Discourse on Job
48.016.p: When Nathaniel and John asked about the reasons for suffering, Jesus explained that suffering is not God's punishment but may be the result of the imperfections of evil, natural accidents, or sin [148:5.3]. Citing the Book of Job, Jesus emphasized that material prosperity is not evidence of divine favor and suffering is not necessarily a punishment for sin [148:6.2]~3. He taught that just as Job achieved victory by obtaining a vision of God amidst suffering, humans can reach heights of moral understanding and spiritual insight through affliction [148:6.3].
48.017.h4: 4) Healing the Paralytic and Authority to Forgive Sins
48.018.p: In the last week at Bethsaida, Jesus healed a paralytic let down through the roof, declaring, "Your sins are forgiven" [148:9.2]. This was to show the Pharisees that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, and due to this event, some Pharisee spies converted and were baptized [148:9.3][148:9.4].
48.019.h3: 3. Characteristics and Teachings of the Second Preaching Tour
48.020.h4: 1) Scale of the Tour and Spontaneous Healing Phenomena
48.021.p: The second preaching tour, which began on October 3, A.D. 28, included Jesus, the twelve apostles, and 117 newly trained evangelists, visiting many cities like Gadara and Megiddo [149:0.1]. A feature of this tour was that unexplained spontaneous healings occurred even though Jesus did not intentionally perform miracles [149:1.1]~2. These healings were a phenomenon resulting from the combination of strong human faith, the healing power of the Creator Son, and the Father's will, occurring without Jesus' conscious intent [149:1.5]~6.
48.023.p: Jesus understood the human mind, was free from superstition and prejudice, and valued reality over tradition and a clean heart over clean hands [149:2.1][149:2.11]. He taught that anger indicates a failure of the spiritual nature to control, emphasizing the importance of a balanced personality and warning against the dangers of overspecialization, fanaticism, or excessive prudence [149:4.2]~4. Jesus came to preach love instead of fear and joy instead of sorrow, teaching that God should be served as a loving Father, not feared as a King [149:6.2][149:6.8].
48.025.p: In contrast to Jesus' rising fame and welcome among the common people, the religious leaders in Jerusalem showed increasing hostility [149:3.1]. The conversion of young Abraham and the baptism of the spies particularly alarmed them, and they became convinced that Jesus must be executed as a religious offender [149:3.2]`.
48.026.h3: 4. The Third Preaching Tour and the Beginning of Women's Ministry
48.027.h4: 1) Establishment and Activities of the Women's Evangelistic Corps
48.028.p: The most revolutionary event of the third preaching tour was Jesus' official commissioning of ten women as ministers of the kingdom [150:1.1]. This women's corps, including Susanna, Joanna, Martha, and Mary Magdalene, organized themselves and financed their own work of preaching the gospel [150:1.1]~2. This broke the custom of the times when women were not even admitted to the main floor of the synagogue, declaring spiritual freedom for women and confirming them as equal children of God with men [150:1.3]. Mary Magdalene, in particular, became one of the most effective evangelists, and the women achieved great success in approaching the sick and entering places of ill repute [150:2.2]~3.
48.029.h4: 2) Breaking Superstitions and Teachings on Salvation
48.030.p: At Tiberias, Jesus refuted prevalent superstitions such as astrology, amulets, dream interpretation, and magic point by point, emphasizing that the only way to communicate with the spiritual world is through indwelling spiritual endowments [150:3.2][150:3.7]. Regarding the question "What shall I do to be saved?", Jesus taught to believe the gospel of the kingdom, accept divine forgiveness, and recognize sonship with God through faith [150:5.2]. He clarified that salvation is God's gift and that a righteous life is the natural fruit of the saved, not a condition for salvation [150:5.5].
48.031.h4: 3) Dispatching Apostles and Rejection at Nazareth
48.032.p: Jesus sent the apostles out two by two throughout Galilee, instructing them to go to the lost sheep of Israel rather than to Gentile cities or Samaria [150:4.1]~2. At the end of the tour, Jesus visited his hometown of Nazareth, but the people there rejected and antagonized him instead of welcoming him [150:7.2]. In the synagogue service, Jesus read from Isaiah and proclaimed himself the fulfillment of that prophecy, but the people scoffed at "the son of Joseph" and demanded miracles [150:9.1]~2. The angry mob even tried to push Jesus off a cliff to kill him, but he passed through their midst with dignity, and this event brought the third preaching tour to a bitter close [150:9.3][150:9.5].
48.033.h3: 5. The Faith of Jesus and Its Importance
48.035.p: Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God, which was not traditional or intellectual but wholly personal and spiritual [196:0.1]. He viewed God not as a stern judge but as a loving Father and never lost assurance of God's guidance even amidst adversity [196:0.2]~3. Jesus' faith combined the pure trust of a child with the strong intellectual courage of an adult, maintaining unshakable serenity even in uncertain situations [196:0.11]~12.
48.036.h4: 2) The Importance of Living the Religion of Jesus
48.037.p: We must share the faith of Jesus beyond merely having faith in Jesus [196:1.3]. Jesus did not ask his disciples just to believe in him, but to believe with him and trust in the reality of God's love [196:0.13]. True religion should not be theological doctrines about Jesus but a religion of personal experience in doing the Father's will and serving human brothers, as Jesus demonstrated [196:2.6]. Jesus' life is a living way showing that humans can start from the lowest spiritual level and reach the highest level of divine values [196:2.4]. The greatest challenge for modern man is to communicate with the divine Monitor indwelling the human mind and achieve God-consciousness like Jesus [196:3.34].
49.title: Jesus' Last Week
49.001.h3: 1. Monday: Cleansing the Temple and Challenges to Authority
49.002.h4: 1) Cleansing the Temple and Indignation at Commercialism
49.003.p: Jesus and the apostles arrived at the temple in Jerusalem early Monday morning from Bethany, where Jesus observed the widespread selling of sacrificial animals and commercial exchange by money-changers in the temple courts [173:1.1]. Since this traffic profaned the temple worship and was a scheme to exploit the poor for massive profits, Jesus, filled with indignation, drove out the animals and overturned the money-changers' tables, declaring, "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples, but you have made it a den of robbers" [173:1.7]. This event revealed the Master's attitude toward the commercialization of religious practices and his detestation of unfair exploitation, which further solidified the chief priests' determination to kill him [173:1.9].
49.004.h4: 2) Challenges to Authority and Warning Parables
49.005.p: After the cleansing of the temple, the Jewish leaders challenged Jesus' authority, asking, "By what authority do you do these things?" but Jesus avoided their trap and exposed their hypocrisy by asking them in return whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men [173:2.4][173:2.7]. Subsequently, through the parables of the Two Sons, the Wicked Tenants, and the Marriage Feast, Jesus warned that the Jewish leaders had rejected the prophets without repentance and that, as a result, the kingdom of heaven would be taken from them and given to others [173:4.4][173:5.2]. In particular, his statement that "he who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces, but on whomsoever it falls, it will scatter him as dust" was a stern warning of the spiritual crisis they faced [173:4.4].
49.006.h3: 2. Tuesday: The Last Public Discourse and Prophecies on the Mount of Olives
49.007.h4: 1) Questioning by Jewish Leaders and Wise Answers
49.008.p: On Tuesday morning, Jesus faced a united attack in the temple from Pharisees, Sadducees, and Herodians, who tried to entrap him with questions about taxes, the resurrection, and the greatest commandment [174:2.1]. Jesus avoided the political trap by answering to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's, and he pointed out the error of the Sadducees regarding the resurrection by proclaiming that God is the God of the living [174:2.2]. Regarding the greatest commandment, he clearly taught that it is to love God with all one's heart and to love one's neighbor as oneself, encouraging the lawyer that he was not far from the kingdom of God [174:4.2]~3.
49.009.h4: 2) The Last Public Discourse and Indictment of Hypocrisy
49.010.p: After the questioning ended, Jesus boldly criticized the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees, and with seven "woes," he made his final break with the Jewish leaders and left the temple [175:1.24]. Jesus denounced them for appearing holy on the outside while being full of greed and self-indulgence on the inside, and for shutting the kingdom of heaven against men [175:1.12]. This sermon was his last appeal to the Jewish people and a final indictment of their false teachers and narrow-minded leaders [175:0.1].
49.011.h4: 3) Prophecies on the Mount of Olives and Teachings on the Second Coming
49.012.p: After leaving the temple, Jesus taught the disciples on the Mount of Olives regarding the destruction of Jerusalem and his second coming, distinguishing the destruction of Jerusalem as a political event to occur within a generation from the second coming of the Son of Man as a spiritual event of unknown timing [176:1.1][176:2.6]. The disciples confused these two events, trying to connect the end of the world with the arrival of the New Jerusalem, but Jesus emphasized that the gospel must be preached to all nations and, through the parable of the talents, urged them to be faithful to their trust until the Master comes [176:3.4]. Jesus taught that living one's earthly life faithfully in the spirit is the surest way to prepare for the future, stating, "If my words abide in you, you are my disciples indeed".
49.013.h3: 3. Wednesday: Rest and the Plot of Betrayal
49.014.h4: 1) Rest with John Mark and the Importance of Family Life
49.015.p: Wednesday was a day when Jesus ceased official activities and rested with his disciples; he spent the day in the hills with the young John Mark, talking to him about boyhood and the importance of family life [177:1.3]. Jesus emphasized how important a home environment balanced with love and wisdom is for sound character formation, expressing confidence that John Mark would become a mighty gospel messenger thanks to his excellent upbringing [177:2.2]. This time was a peaceful day spent with God, showing that the Creator is willing to fellowship with his creatures [177:1.3].
49.017.p: While Jesus spent a peaceful time, Judas Iscariot left Jesus and the apostles to meet with the high priest Caiaphas to plot betrayal [177:4.1]. Driven by disappointment that Jesus was not the political liberator of Israel, a sense of personal humiliation, and selfish motives to secure his own safety and glory, Judas agreed to hand Jesus over to his enemies [177:4.9]. Judas realized that Jesus' power was not gone but that he would not use it for himself, and he decided to seek rewards from the old order rather than remain with a defeated movement [177:4.3][177:4.9].
49.018.h3: 4. Thursday: The Last Supper and Prayer in Gethsemane
49.019.h4: 1) The Last Supper and the Example of Service
49.020.p: On Thursday evening, Jesus held the last Passover supper with his apostles in the upper room of Mark's home, where he washed the disciples' feet, personally demonstrating the lesson of humility and service that "he who would be greatest among you must become the server of all" [179:3.9]. This was a practical teaching regarding the apostles' disputes over who was the greatest and their refusal to wash feet [179:1.4][179:3.8]. Afterward, Jesus instituted a new supper by sharing bread and wine, a symbol of the new era of remembering his life in the flesh and his words of eternal truth, and of communing in the spirit [179:5.9].
49.021.h4: 2) The New Commandment and the Promise of the Comforter
49.022.p: After supper, Jesus gave the new commandment, "Love one another as I have loved you," and promised that after he left, the Spirit of Truth, the Comforter, would come to guide them into all truth [180:1.1][180:4.1]. Jesus explained that he is the vine and the disciples are the branches, emphasizing that they can bear fruit only when they abide in him [180:2.1]. He explained that it was expedient for him to go away in the flesh so that the Spirit of Truth could indwell each of their hearts [180:6.2].
49.024.p: Arriving at the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed three times in extreme agony, "Not my will, but yours be done," overcoming human fear and demonstrating complete submission to God's will [182:3.4]. While the disciples fell asleep unable to overcome their fatigue, Jesus decided alone to drink the cup of suffering for the salvation of humanity [182:3.6]. He determined to walk that path as a complete human without using his divine powers, even amidst the pain where his sweat fell like drops of blood [182:3.7].
49.025.h3: 5. Friday: Trial and the Way of the Cross
49.026.h4: 1) Arrest and Interrogation in the Jewish Courts
49.027.p: Early Friday morning, Jesus was arrested by armed soldiers led by the betrayer Judas; Jesus boldly revealed his identity, protected his disciples, and submitted to arrest. He was first taken to the former high priest Annas for interrogation, then to Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin for an illegal trial [184:1.1][184:3.1]. When the testimonies of false witnesses did not agree, Caiaphas asked, "Are you the Son of God?" and when Jesus answered, "I am," they condemned him to death for blasphemy [184:3.15]. Peter followed at a distance but was seized with fear, denied Jesus three times, and wept bitterly [184:2.8].
49.028.h4: 2) Trial Before Pilate and the Sentence of the Cross
49.029.p: Since the Jewish leaders had no authority to execute, they took Jesus to the Roman governor Pilate; Pilate found no fault in Jesus and tried to release him but feared the tumult of the crowd [185:2.16]. Pilate tried to evade responsibility by sending Jesus to Herod, but Herod only mocked Jesus and sent him back [185:4.3]. Eventually, yielding to the crowd's demand to release the murderer Barabbas and the threats regarding his loyalty to Caesar, Pilate handed over the innocent Jesus to be crucified [185:8.2]. Throughout this process, Jesus maintained silence and dignity, showing the example of perfect obedience amidst human wickedness and God's will [186:2.3].
49.030.h4: 3) Judas's End and the True Meaning of the Cross
49.031.p: Judas Iscariot, realizing his betrayal had driven Jesus to death, belatedly regretted his actions, threw the silver coins into the temple, and ended his life by suicide [186:1.7]. Jesus carried the cross to Golgotha; this was not a sacrifice required by God to wash away human sin, but a tragedy caused by human wickedness, through which Jesus revealed God's love and his complete devotion to human salvation [186:5.2]. Jesus' death occurred at the time of the slaughter of the Passover lambs, but this was not related to the Jewish sacrificial system but was a universal event revealing God to humanity and leading humanity to God [186:5.6].
49.032.h3: 6. The Meaning of Jesus' Last Week
49.034.p: Jesus' last week was not merely a process toward a tragic death, but a time of completing the revelation of the Father's love and truth shown throughout his life. By cleansing the temple and rebuking hypocritical leaders, he established the uncompromising authority of truth, and by washing the disciples' feet and giving the new commandment, he taught that service and love are the core values of the kingdom of heaven [180:1.1]. The prayer in Gethsemane showed the pinnacle of faith aligning human will with God's will, and the way of the cross proved the victory of the divine character that forgives and loves without retaliation even in the face of injustice and suffering [182:3.6].
49.035.h4: 2) Opening of a New Spiritual Era
49.036.p: Facing death, Jesus declared to his disciples, "I have overcome the world," urging them not to lose peace amidst tribulation [181:1.5]. He promised that although he was leaving in the flesh, he would be with them forever through the Spirit of Truth, signifying that Jesus' life and death were not an end but the beginning of a new spiritual era [180:4.1]. Jesus' last week left us an example of triumphant faith that maintains absolute trust in God and love for humanity even amidst the deepest betrayal, loneliness, and suffering a human can experience [196:0.3].
50.title: The Meaning of the Cross
50.001.h3: 1. Differences between Christian Atonement Doctrine and the Cross in The Urantia Book
50.002.h4: 1) Refutation of Traditional Atonement and the True Nature of God
50.003.p: The Urantia Book fundamentally interprets the traditional atonement doctrine—the concept that Jesus became a sacrificial offering to pay for the sins of humanity—differently. Jesus did not die to atone for the racial guilt of mortal man nor to provide an effective approach to an angry and offended God [188:4.1]. The Son of Man did not offer himself as a sacrifice to appease the wrath of God and to open the way for sinful man to obtain salvation; these ideas of atonement and propitiation are erroneous [188:4.1]. To view God as an austere and all-powerful monarch who delights in seeing his subjects punished unless someone else suffers in their stead is a primitive concept, and it is incompatible with the concept of the loving Father that Jesus demonstrated [188:4.8]. The Father in heaven treats his children as a wise earthly father; he disciplines for love and correction, not in anger or for vengeance [188:4.10].
50.004.h4: 2) The True Purpose of the Cross and the Concept of Salvation
50.005.p: The cross was not a sacrifice to pay a debt which God held against mankind, nor did Jesus die to rescue men from the clutch of fallen rulers [188:4.3]. While these concepts of atonement and sacrificial salvation are rooted in selfishness, Jesus taught that the highest concept of the brotherhood of the spirit believers is unselfish service to one's fellows [188:4.9]. While it may not be proper to speak of Jesus as a sacrificer or a redeemer, it is wholly correct to refer to him as a Savior, for he forever made the way of salvation more plain and certain [188:4.7]. The cross stands not as a symbol of the appeasement of the wrath of an offended God by the sacrifice of an innocent Son, but as a symbol of the salvation of the bad by the loving devotion of the good, standing forever as such a symbol in a vast universe [188:5.9].
50.006.h4: 3) Revelation of Love Rather than Reconciliation with God
50.007.p: It is clear that the death of Jesus on the cross was not to reconcile man to God but to stimulate man to realize the eternal love of God and the mercy of his Son, and to broadcast this universal truth to a whole universe [188:5.13]. The cross reveals not condemnation or condonation of sin but the salvation of eternal love, presenting not merely justice but a higher inherent righteousness [188:5.2]. Divine love does not merely forgive wrongs; it absorbs and actually destroys them, implying rehabilitation and eternal survival [188:5.2]. Therefore, salvation should be taken for granted by those who believe in the fatherhood of God, and the believer's chief concern should not be the selfish desire for personal salvation but the unselfish urge to love and serve one's fellows [188:4.9].
50.008.h3: 2. Jesus' Extreme Suffering and the Perfection of Human Existence
50.009.h4: 1) Rejection of Supernatural Power and Death as a Complete Human
50.010.p: The reason Jesus suffered such extreme pain in Gethsemane and on the cross is that he elected to live without recourse to supernatural power and to die as an ordinary mortal [187:3.6]. He walked to the crucifixion very weary and nearly exhausted; he had had no food or water since the Last Supper at the home of Elijah Mark, nor had he been permitted to sleep for one moment [187:1.8]. Furthermore, he had been subjected to a severe scourging with its associated suffering and loss of blood, all superimposed upon extreme mental anguish, acute spiritual tension, and a sense of human loneliness [187:1.8]. Despite these physical and mental limitations, he desired to accept the human experience to the full and to overcome it [187:2.3].
50.011.h4: 2) Maintaining Human Consciousness and Assurance of the Father's Will
50.012.p: Jesus refused the narcotic wine offered by the Jewish women to deaden the pain, choosing to maintain his human consciousness until the end [187:2.3]. Crucifixion was a cruel and lingering punishment, yet Jesus, though thirsty, refused to drink the drugged wine [187:2.3]. This was because he lived as a man and intended to die as a man, fulfilling the Father's will [187:3.6]. During the approaching hour of death, the human mind of Jesus resorted to the repetition of many passages from the Psalms; he never for one moment doubted that he had lived in accordance with the Father's will, nor did he doubt that he was now laying down his life in the flesh in accordance with that will [187:5.2]. He did not feel that the Father had forsaken him; he was merely reciting in his vanishing consciousness scriptures such as the twenty-second Psalm [187:5.2].
50.013.h4: 3) The Kingly Attitude Toward the Cross and the Final Expression of Love
50.014.p: In reality, Jesus of Nazareth had borne the cross of a real and intense human existence for more than twenty-five years, and the real value of the cross consists in the fact that it was the supreme and final expression of his love and the completed revelation of his mercy. In enriching human experience and enlarging the way of salvation, it is not the fact of his death but the superb manner and the matchless spirit in which he met death that is important [188:4.12]. Jesus lived as a king and died as a king; he willingly admitted his kingship and remained master of the situation throughout the tragic day [187:5.6]. Men need not fear that the Creator does not know the nature or extent of their temporal afflictions; even if they do not understand Jesus, they can at least understand his fellowship of mortal suffering [188:5.12].
50.015.h3: 3. Our Attitude toward the Cross and the True Meaning of the Cross
50.016.h4: 1) Establishment of the Family Relationship and Symbol of Devotion
50.017.p: We should accept the cross as the symbol establishing forever that all relationships between God and man are the family relations of father and son. The central truth of the Creator-creature relationship is the love of a father for his son, not the justice of a king seeking satisfaction in the punishment of an evil-doing subject [188:5.1]. The cross shows how much the true shepherd is devoted to his flock, even the unworthy members [188:5.1]. We must be careful not to view the cross with the eyes of primitive men or later barbarians, but rather see in it Jesus' final expression of love and devotion to his life mission [188:5.11]. The Father required nothing of the cross; Jesus gave it willingly and refused to avoid it [188:5.11].
50.018.h4: 2) Inspiration for Unselfish Service and Overcoming Complaints
50.019.p: The cross is the symbol of the highest form of unselfish service, the supreme expression of the complete bestowal of a righteous life [188:5.9]. The mere contemplation of this great symbol of the bestowal of the life of Jesus inspires all of us to want to live as he lived [188:5.9]. When thinking men and women look upon Jesus offering up his life on the cross, they will hardly again permit themselves to complain at even the severest hardships of life, much less at petty harassments or fictitious grievances [188:5.10]. On millions of inhabited worlds, tens of trillions of creatures tempted to give up the moral struggle have taken one more look at Jesus on the cross and have been inspired to forge ahead [188:5.5].
50.020.h4: 3) The Victory of Love and Truth Over Hate and Evil
50.021.p: The triumph of the death on the cross is epitomized in the spirit of Jesus toward his assailants when he prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do," making the cross an eternal symbol of the triumph of love over hate and the victory of truth over evil [188:5.6]. This devotion of love was contagious throughout a vast universe, and the disciples caught it from their Master [188:5.6]. The cross makes a supreme appeal to the best in man because it discloses one who was willing to lay down his life for his fellow men [188:5.7]. Greater love no man has than this, that he would lay down his life for his friends; and Jesus had such a love that he was willing to lay down his life for his enemies [188:5.7].
50.022.h3: 4. Important Stories to Address Regarding the Crucifixion Event
50.023.h4: 1) Simon Carrying the Cross and the Inscription
50.024.p: The events on the way to the cross and at Golgotha reveal both the humanity and divinity of Jesus. Customarily, soldiers placed the crossbeam on Jesus' shoulders, but when he fell from exhaustion, they compelled Simon of Cyrene, a passerby, to carry it [187:1.1], 187:1.9. Simon later became a believer in the gospel of the kingdom, and his sons became teachers, though Simon himself never knew that the Jesus whose burden he bore was the very same person as the Jewish teacher whom he had once befriended when his son was injured [187:1.10]. Additionally, the caption placed on the cross by Pilate, "Jesus of Nazareth—the King of the Jews," was a petty revenge to humiliate the Jewish leaders, but it unwittingly proclaimed the truth [187:1.3], 187:2.5.
50.025.h4: 2) The Repentant Thief and the Promise of Immediate Salvation
50.026.p: The story of the thief on the cross is a decisive scene showing the nature of salvation. Unlike the thief who railed at Jesus, the other admitted his sin and asked Jesus, "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom" [187:4.1]. Even in the agony of death, Jesus had time for the confession of the believing thief and promised, "Today I tell you, you shall sometime be with me in Paradise" [187:4.1]. This thief, who had looked upon Barabbas as a hero, saw a true hero on the cross and accepted the Master's teaching in the final hour of consciousness [187:4.2], 187:4.5. This demonstrates that Jesus' love offers immediate salvation to those who believe [187:4.2].
50.027.h4: 3) Consideration in the Final Moments and Evidence of a Righteous Death
50.028.p: Jesus' final moments and his care for his family must not be overlooked. Even on the cross, he committed his mother Mary to John, saying, "Woman, behold your son!" and to John, "Son, behold your mother!" fulfilling his human duties and love to the end [187:4.7]. When Jesus cried out, "It is finished! Father, into your hands I commend my spirit," and gave up his life, the Roman centurion confessed, "This was indeed a righteous man; truly he must have been a Son of God" [187:5.5]. The body of Jesus was cared for by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, who took it to Joseph's new family tomb, signifying that they had left the Sanhedrin to become open disciples of Jesus [188:1.2].
50.029.h3: 5. The Faith of Jesus and the Path We Must Follow
50.030.h4: 1) Sharing the Faith of Jesus Beyond Faith in Jesus
50.031.p: We must have the faith of Jesus, beyond merely having faith in Jesus. Jesus did not require his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him, trusting in the reality of God's love and the assurance of sonship [196:0.13]. Jesus' faith was not traditional or merely intellectual; it was wholly personal and purely spiritual [196:0.1]. To "follow Jesus" means to personally share his religious faith and to enter into the spirit of the Master's life of unselfish service for man [196:1.3]. The goal of the believers of the kingdom is not to literally imitate the outward life of Jesus, but to trust God as he trusted God and to believe in men as he believed in men [196:1.5].
50.032.h4: 2) Faith Combining Childlike Trust and Adult Courage
50.033.p: Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God, experiencing tranquility in the supreme trust of God even in the face of all the natural difficulties and temporal contradictions of mortal existence [196:0.1], 196:0.3. His faith was trustful like a child's but never childish; it combined the strong and intelligent courage of a full-grown man with the sincere and trusting optimism of a believing child [196:0.11]. Jesus had a wholehearted faith in the fundamental goodness of the universe, resembling a child's trust in the security of his earthly surroundings [196:0.11]. This triumphant faith was a living experience of actual spiritual attainment, and Jesus' great contribution to human experience was his superb human portrayal of a new and higher type of living faith in God [196:0.3].
50.034.h4: 3) Personal Religious Experience and Communication with God
50.035.p: Ultimately, the core lesson of the cross and Jesus' life is the importance of personal religious experience. Jesus founded a religion of personal experience in doing the will of God and serving the human brotherhood [196:2.6]. The earthly life of Jesus was devoted to one great purpose—doing the Father's will [196:0.14]. The greatest challenge for modern man is to achieve better communication with the divine Monitor that dwells within the human mind [196:3.34]. The God revealed to the world through Jesus will not fail, and human evolution is still in progress [196:3.33]. We must choose to believe in the love of God revealed through the cross of Jesus and, within that love, take up our own cross and live following the faith of Jesus.
51.title: The Teachings of Jesus
51.001.h3: 1. The Father in Heaven and the Relationship with God
51.002.h4: 1) God as a Father of Love and Mercy
51.003.p: The foundation of Jesus' teaching was to fundamentally change the concept of God; he taught that God is not a fearsome judge or a stern monarch, but a "living and loving Father in heaven" [196:0.2]. Jesus portrayed God not only as holy, just, and great, but also as true, beautiful, and good, concentrating all attributes of divinity in the mind as the "will of the Father in heaven" [196:0.2]. The relationship between God and man is not a legal one but a family relationship, and divine forgiveness is inevitable, inherent in God's infinite understanding and knowledge of the immaturity of his children [174:1.3]. Jesus taught that the Father views the immaturity of the child in the light of deeper experience, and that divine justice is eternally fair and always includes the mercy of understanding [174:1.3].
51.004.h4: 2) Sonship with God and Eternal Life
51.005.p: Jesus exalted the concept of God to a sublime experience by proclaiming the fact that every mortal creature is a child of this loving Father, a son of God [196:0.2]. He defined eternal life as knowing the Father, the only true God, and believing in him whom he sent [182:1.3]. Salvation is a gift given to those who accept sonship with God through faith, and this relationship is an intimate and loving one between the creature and the Creator [174:1.2]. Jesus revealed the Father's name to the world through his life, and that name was revealed as the Bread of Life, the Living Water, the Light of the World, the Good Shepherd, and the Resurrection and the Life [182:1.10][182:1.16][182:1.18].
51.006.h4: 3) The Indwelling Spirit and the Father's Will
51.007.p: Jesus taught that God is not a distant entity but dwells within us; he promised that the Father's spirit is already in your hearts and that when the Spirit of Truth comes, he will dwell within you [180:4.1]. Faith is not merely intellectual assent but an insight born of the activity of the indwelling Adjuster, and to one who knows God, all ordinary labor becomes sacred service to the Father [196:0.1][181:2.19]. In Jesus' teachings, religion was consistently interpreted as doing the Father's will, which means dedicating one's own will to the majestic service of doing the divine will [196:0.10].
51.008.h3: 2. The Nature of the Kingdom of Heaven (Kingdom of God) and Citizenship
51.009.h4: 1) The Kingdom as a Spiritual Brotherhood
51.010.p: Jesus taught that the kingdom of heaven is fundamentally different from the material kingdoms of this world; it is a spiritual brotherhood of spiritual sons born of God [178:1.2]. He testified to Pilate that "My kingdom is not of this world," clarifying that if it were, his disciples would have fought, thus establishing that the kingdom is a spiritual dominion [185:3.3]. The kingdom of heaven is not a visible external organization, but a kingdom of brotherhood where men become sons of God through faith and love, and this salvation is for Gentiles as well as Jews [185:3.3]. The kingdom is like leaven in dough and like a mustard seed, growing like the seed of a living being, adapting to the needs of each generation [178:1.15].
51.011.h4: 2) Relationship with Worldly Kingdoms and Civic Duty
51.012.p: Jesus taught, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's," clarifying that there is no inherent conflict between sonship in the spiritual kingdom and citizenship in earthly governments [174:2.2][178:1.3]. Believers must not render spiritual worship to earthly rulers nor use physical force to advance the spiritual kingdom, but at the same time, they should be ideal citizens of the kingdoms of this world [178:1.3][178:1.4]. The believer in the kingdom faces a double responsibility of duty to man and duty to God, and must shed spiritual light upon the sons of darkness through unselfish social service [178:1.4]~5.
51.013.h4: 3) Conditions and Attitude for Entering the Kingdom
51.014.p: Jesus taught that whoever wishes to be great in the kingdom of heaven must become like a child, and whoever wishes to be first must become a server [179:3.9]. Entering the kingdom is a spiritual and personal matter, experienced in the spirit solely through the realization of the faith that one is a son of God [176:3.2]. One who knows God and believes the gospel has already received the assurance of eternal life and is not shaken by external upheavals such as the end of the world or the collapse of empires [176:3.2]. Jesus emphasized that the gospel of the kingdom must be preached to all nations, and believers have received the mandate to proclaim the joy and liberty of knowing God [178:1.11].
51.015.h3: 3. Brotherly Love and the New Commandment
51.016.h4: 1) The New Commandment to Love One Another
51.017.p: At the Last Supper, Jesus gave his disciples a new commandment: "Love one another as I have loved you" [180:1.1]. This goes beyond the old commandment to "love your neighbor as yourself," demanding a higher level of love that takes Jesus' love as the standard [180:1.1]. There is no greater love than for a man to lay down his life for his friends, and Jesus called his disciples friends, not servants, urging them to practice this love [180:1.3]. Only when we love one another will the world know that we are Jesus' disciples [180:1.1].
51.019.p: Love must appear not as an abstract emotion but as concrete service; Jesus personally demonstrated the truth that "he who would be greatest among you must become the server of all" by washing his disciples' feet himself [179:3.8]~9. Jesus taught that since he, the Lord and Master, washed their feet, they should also wash one another's feet, emphasizing that greatness in the spiritual kingdom lies not in ruling but in humble service [179:3.8]. Loving service should not stem from a sense of duty but from the joy of serving friends, which is the way to share Jesus' joy [180:1.5]~6.
51.020.h4: 3) Spiritual Interpretation of the Golden Rule
51.021.p: Jesus taught the Golden Rule, "Do to others as you would have them do to you," not as a simple ethical rule but on the level of spiritual realization [180:5.7]. To a God-knowing person, the Golden Rule becomes an ideal of spiritual reality that is satisfied only when we love others as Jesus loved us [180:5.8]. Love and unselfishness are not fixed rules but living adaptabilities that must be constantly reinterpreted under the guidance of the Spirit of Truth [180:5.10].
51.022.h3: 4. The Spirit of Truth and Living Faith
51.023.h4: 1) The Promise of the Spirit of Truth
51.024.p: Jesus promised to send the "Spirit of Truth" after he left; this new teacher is not a dead letter of law or doctrine but living truth itself, dwelling in the human heart and guiding into all truth [180:5.1][180:4.1]. The Spirit of Truth enables Jesus to be with his disciples more completely than when he was in the flesh, teaching about sin and righteousness and bringing to remembrance all that Jesus taught [180:4.2]~3. This Spirit is Jesus' spiritual presence, acting to comfort and guide believers, not leaving them as orphans [180:4.1].
51.025.h4: 2) The Parable of the Vine and Branches
51.026.p: Jesus taught the living spiritual connection between the believer and himself through the parable, "I am the vine, you are the branches" [180:2.1]. Just as a branch cannot bear fruit unless it abides in the vine, believers cannot bear the fruit of loving service unless they abide in Jesus [180:2.1]. Through communion with the indwelling Spirit, the believer bears much fruit, and this is the way to glorify the Father [180:2.1]. Prayer is not enforcing one's own will, but a process of accepting God's will and aligning with it, just as the life of the vine flows into the branches [180:2.4].
51.027.h4: 3) Difference Between Living Truth and Fixed Doctrine
51.028.p: Jesus taught that truth is not confined in static formulas or creeds but is a dynamic and living reality [180:5.2]. Truth is not something to be learned but lived; it is not to be understood with the head but experienced in the heart [180:5.2]. Jesus did not want his teachings to crystallize into dead truth but desired the Spirit of Truth to illuminate and expand the truth anew to meet the needs of each generation [178:1.15].
51.030.h4: 1) Peace Unlike What the World Gives
51.031.p: Jesus told his disciples, "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you," stating that this is not the peace the world gives [181:1.5]. Jesus' peace is not a vague optimism that everything will be fine, nor is it a stoicism that suppresses emotions; it is the peace of a son that comes from absolute trust in the wise and loving care of the Universal Father [181:1.7][181:1.10]. This peace stems from the assurance that one is doing the will of God and provides unwavering serenity even in the face of death.
51.032.h4: 2) Tribulation in the World and Victory
51.033.p: Jesus warned that disciples would have tribulation in the world but encouraged them, saying, "Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world" [181:1.6]. The world will hate and persecute the disciples as it hated Jesus, because they do not belong to the world [180:3.1]. Jesus taught not to resist evil with violence, for those who take the sword perish by the sword, and the spiritual kingdom can be proclaimed only by the power of the spirit [183:3.7][178:1.2].
51.034.h4: 3) Hope and Preparation for the Future
51.035.p: Jesus promised to go to the Father to prepare a place for the disciples, teaching that in the Father's house are many mansions [180:3.4]. He will come again to receive the disciples, which includes not only a return in the flesh but also his spiritual presence and the ascent after death [181:1.5]. Jesus warned of future disasters like the destruction of Jerusalem, urging them to watch, not be deceived, and possess their souls in patience [176:1.1]. The important thing is not knowing the day or the hour, but being a faithful steward of the assigned work so as to be ready to welcome the Master whenever he comes [176:3.4].
52.title: The Religion of Jesus and the Religion About Jesus
52.001.h3: 1. The Transition of the Gospel: From the Message of Jesus to the Doctrine About Jesus
52.002.h4: 1) Pentecost and the Shift of Focus
52.003.p: When the 120 believers were engaged in prayer, about one o'clock, they all became conscious of a strange presence in the room, and at the same time, these disciples became aware of a new and profound sense of spiritual joy, security, and confidence [194:0.1]. This consciousness of a new spiritual strength was immediately followed by a strong urge to go out and publicly proclaim the gospel of the kingdom and the good news that Jesus had risen from the dead [194:0.1]. These men had been trained and instructed that they were to preach the fatherhood of God and the sonship of man, but at just this moment of spiritual ecstasy and personal triumph, the best news, the greatest thought which these men could think, was the fact of the risen Master [194:0.3]. So they went out, endowed with power from on high, preaching glad tidings to the people—even salvation through Jesus—but they unintentionally stumbled into the error of substituting some of the facts associated with the gospel for the gospel message itself [194:0.3]. The gospel of the kingdom is: the fact of the fatherhood of God, coupled with the resultant truth of the sonship-brotherhood of men; Christianity, as it developed from that day, is: the fact of God as the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, in association with the experience of believer-fellowship with the risen and glorified Christ [194:0.4]. Peter unintentionally began this mistake, and others furthered it, up to Paul, who created a new religion based on the new version of the good news [194:0.3].
52.004.h4: 2) Differences Between the Religion of Jesus and Christianity
52.005.p: Some day a reformation in the Christian church may be deep enough to get back to the unadulterated religious teachings of Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, but currently, while one may preach a religion about Jesus, such a believer is likely to remain content to talk about him and not live the religion of Jesus [196:2.1].
