The gospel of the kingdom is founded on the personal religious experience of the Jesus of Galilee; Christianity is founded almost exclusively on the personal religious experience of the Apostle Paul [196:2.1]. Jesus founded the religion of personal experience in doing the will of God and serving the human brotherhood; Paul founded a religion in which the glorified Jesus became the object of worship and the brotherhood consisted of fellow believers in the divine Christ [196:2.6]. In the bestowal of Jesus, these two concepts were potential in his divine-human life, and it is indeed a pity that his followers failed to create a unified religion that might have given proper recognition to both the human and the divine natures of the Master [196:2.6]. The greatest mistake made was that, while the human Jesus was recognized as having a religion, the divine Jesus (Christ) almost overnight became a religion [196:2.4]. Paul's Christianity made sure of the adoration of the divine Christ, but it almost wholly lost sight of the struggling and valiant human Jesus of Galilee, who, by the valor of his personal religious faith and the heroism of his indwelling Adjuster, ascended from the lowly levels of humanity to become one with divinity [196:2.4].
52.006.p: 3)Formation of the Early Church and Doctrinal Changes
52.007.p: After Pentecost, the message of Jesus regarding the kingdom was suddenly changed into the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ [194:4.5]. They now proclaimed the facts of his life, death, and resurrection and preached the hope of his speedy return to this world to finish the work he began [194:4.5]. Christ became the creed of the rapidly forming church; Jesus lived in their hearts, and he dominated their thinking and determined their new concept of God and everything else [194:4.6]. They were too much excited about the new doctrine that "God is the Father of the Lord Jesus" to be concerned with the old message that "God is the loving Father of all men" [194:4.6]. True, a marvelous manifestation of brotherly love and unparalleled good will sprang up in these early communities of believers, but it was a fellowship of believers in Jesus, not a fellowship of brothers in the family kingdom of the Father in Paradise [194:4.6]. The kingdom of heaven in the teachings of Jesus was the spiritual ideal of individual righteousness and divine fellowship, but this was gradually submerged by the mystical concept of the person of Jesus as the Redeemer-Creator and spiritual head of a socialized religious community [170:5.9]. In this way, a formal and institutionalized church became the substitute for the kingdom of spirit-led brotherhood [170:5.9].
52.008.h3: 2. The Core of Jesus' Religion: Personal Experience and Faith
52.010.p: Jesus enjoyed a sublime and wholehearted faith in God; he experienced the ordinary ups and downs of mortal existence, but he never religiously doubted the certainty of God's watchcare and guidance [196:0.1]. Jesus' faith was not traditional or merely intellectual; it was wholly personal and purely spiritual [196:0.1]. The human Jesus saw God as being holy, just, and great, as well as being true, beautiful, and good [196:0.2]. All these attributes of divinity he focused in his mind as the "will of the Father in heaven" [196:0.2]. Jesus did not cling to faith in God as would a struggling soul at war with the universe and at death grips with a hostile and sinful world [196:0.3]. He experienced the tranquility of supreme trust in God even in the face of all the natural difficulties and temporal contradictions of mortal existence, and he felt the tremendous thrill of living, by faith, in the very presence of the heavenly Father [196:0.3]. This triumphant faith was a living experience of actual spiritual attainment [196:0.3].
52.012.p: The earthly life of Jesus was devoted to one great purpose—doing the Father's will, living the human life religiously and by faith [196:0.14]. As a man of the realm, Jesus brought to God the greatest of all offerings: the consecration and dedication of his own will to the majestic service of doing the divine will [196:0.10]. Jesus always and consistently interpreted religion wholly in terms of the Father's will [196:0.10]. When you study the career of the Master as concerns prayer or any other feature of the religious life, look not so much for what he taught as for what he did [196:0.10]. Jesus never prayed as a religious duty; to him prayer was a sincere expression of spiritual attitude, a declaration of soul loyalty [196:0.10]. The secret of his unparalleled religious life was this consciousness of the presence of God [196:0.10].
52.014.p: The faith of Jesus was trusting like that of a child, but it was wholly free from presumption [196:0.11]. Jesus trusted God much as the child trusts a parent; he had a profound confidence in the universe—just such a trust as the child has in its parental environment [196:0.11]. He combined the strong and intelligent courage of a full-grown man with the sincere and trusting optimism of a believing child [196:0.11]. Jesus' faith attained the purity of a child's trust; his faith was so absolute and undoubting that it responded to the charm of the contact of fellow beings and to the wonders of the universe [196:0.12]. In the giant intellect of the full-grown man, the faith of the child reigned supreme in all matters relating to the religious consciousness [196:0.12]. Jesus' faith was childlike, but it was never childish [196:0.12].
52.015.h3: 3. The Path We Must Accept and Practice
52.016.h4: 1) The True Meaning of Following Jesus
52.017.p: To "follow Jesus" means to personally share his religious faith and to enter into the spirit of the Master's life of unselfish service for man [196:1.3]. One of the most important things in human living is to find out what Jesus believed, to discover his ideals, and to strive for the achievement of his exalted life purpose [196:1.3]. Jesus did not require his disciples to believe in him but rather to believe with him, to believe in the reality of the love of God and in full confidence to accept the security of the assurance of sonship with the heavenly Father [196:0.13]. The Master desires that all his followers should fully share his transcendent life of faith [196:0.13]. Jesus challenged his followers not only to believe what he believed, but also to believe as he believed [196:0.13]. This is the full significance of his one supreme requirement, "Follow me" [196:0.13]. The believers of the kingdom should aim not to literally imitate the outward life of Jesus, but to share his faith [196:1.5].
52.018.h4: 2) Personal Religious Experience and the Indwelling Spirit
52.019.p: Personal, spiritual religious experience is an efficient solvent for most mortal difficulties [196:3.1]. True religion does not remove or destroy human troubles, but it does dissolve, absorb, illuminate, and transcend them [196:3.1]. Religious faith—the positive leading of the indwelling divine presence—unfailingly enables the God-knowing man to bridge that gulf existing between the intellectual logic which recognizes the Universal First Cause as It and those positive affirmations of the soul which declare this First Cause to be He, the heavenly Father of Jesus' gospel, the personal God of human salvation [196:3.1]. The greatest challenge to modern man is to achieve better communication with the divine Monitor that dwells within the human mind [196:3.34]. Man's greatest adventure in the flesh consists in the well-balanced and sane effort to advance the borders of self-consciousness out through the dim realms of embryonic soul-consciousness in a wholehearted effort to reach the borderland of spirit-consciousness [196:3.34]. Such an experience constitutes the consciousness of God, an experience which mightily confirms the pre-existent truth of the religious experience of knowing God [196:3.34].
52.020.h4: 3) Practice of Positive and Active Faith
52.021.p: The religion of Jesus does not teach you to be passive mystics or colorless ascetics [178:1.14]. You should not become dreamers and drifters, trusting in a fictitious providence to provide even the necessities of life [178:1.14]. You are to be gentle in your dealings with erring mortals, patient in intercourse with ignorant men, and forbearing under provocation; but you are also to be valiant in defense of righteousness, mighty in the promulgation of truth, and aggressive in the preaching of this gospel of the kingdom [178:1.14]. This gospel of the kingdom is a living truth [178:1.15]. It must not become a static tradition. As it passes from one generation to another, it remains the same living seed, but it casts a new and ever-changing foliage, growing to accept and adapt to the peculiar needs and conditions of each generation [178:1.15]. The revelation Jesus gave is a living revelation, and he desires that it bear appropriate fruits in each individual and in each generation in accordance with the laws of spiritual growth, increase, and adaptative development [178:1.15].
52.022.h3: 4. Prospects for the Future and the Task Ahead
52.024.p: The world needs more firsthand religion [195:9.8]. Even Christianity—the best of the religions of the twentieth century—is not only a religion about Jesus, but it is so largely one which men experience secondhand [195:9.8]. If the world could only know Jesus as he really lived on earth and as he actually taught the life-giving gospel, how the world would wake up! [195:9.8]. Modern culture must become spiritually baptized with a new revelation of Jesus' life and be illuminated with a new understanding of his gospel of eternal salvation [195:10.1]. And when Jesus becomes thus lifted up, he will draw all men to himself [195:10.1]. Jesus' disciples should be more than conquerors, even overflowing sources of inspiration and enhanced living to all men [195:10.1]. Religion is only an exalted humanism until it is made divine by the discovery of the reality of the presence of God in personal experience [195:10.1].
52.025.h4: 2) The Future of Christianity and the Religion of Jesus
52.026.p: Christianity faces the doom embodied in its own slogan: "A house divided against itself cannot stand" [195:10.11]. The living Jesus is the only hope of a unification of Christianity [195:10.11]. The true church—the Jesus brotherhood—is invisible, spiritual, and is characterized by unity [195:10.11]. Spiritual unity is the fruit of faith union with the living Jesus [195:10.11]. If Christianity could only grasp more of Jesus' teachings, it could do so much more in helping modern man to solve his new and increasingly complex problems [195:10.19]. The hope of modern Christianity is that it should cease to sponsor the social systems and industrial policies of Western civilization and bow itself in humble submission before the cross it so valiantly extols, there to learn anew from Jesus of Nazareth the greatest truths mortal man can ever hear—the living gospel of the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man [195:10.21]. The great hope of Urantia lies in the possibility of a new revelation of Jesus with a new and enlarged presentation of his saving message which would spiritually unite in loving service the numerous families of his present-day professed followers [195:10.16].
